summary: Explains how to use the BGP-4 multiprotocol extensions, specifically the MP_REACH_NLRI and MP_UNREACH_NLRI attributes, to convey IPv6 routing information between domains.

plainLanguage.summary: The main system routers use to share maps between networks was built for old addresses. This explains how to make it carry the new, longer ones too.

questions: how does bgp-4 carry ipv6 routes
how does bgp carry ipv6 routes
bgp ipv6 next hop link-local address
subtitle: How BGP-4 carries IPv6 routes, and how to build the next hop field when link-local addresses are involved.

tldr.problem: BGP-4 was designed for IPv4, but IPv6 adds scoped unicast addresses, and link-local addresses do not fit the BGP-4 next hop rules.
tldr.mechanism: Using the MP_REACH_NLRI attribute, a speaker puts the global IPv6 next hop in the Network Address of Next Hop field, optionally followed by a link-local address when the peer shares a subnet.
tldr.outcome: BGP-4 can convey IPv6 reachability information with the same procedures as before, plus these address scope rules.

facts.label: Next hop length, global plus link-local

today: RFC 2545 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: BGP-4 Meets IPv6
sections.content:
BGP-4 and path vector routing protocols in general are mostly independent of the address family. The multiprotocol extensions define two attributes, MP_REACH_NLRI and MP_UNREACH_NLRI, to announce and withdraw reachability information. This document defines how to use them for IPv6.

Unless stated otherwise, the normal BGP-4 procedures apply. The most significant difference from IPv4 is that IPv6 introduces scoped unicast addresses and defines when a particular address scope must be used, so the document is mostly about those scope rules.
sections.plainLanguage: The map-sharing system does not care much what kind of address it carries. Only a few small rules about where an address is valid need adding.

sections.title: IPv6 Address Scopes
sections.content:
IPv6 defines three unicast address scopes: global, site-local and link-local. This document does not distinguish global from site-local addresses and calls both global or non-link-local. Administrators must still respect scope restrictions, and a BGP-4 routing domain and a site are orthogonal notions.

Other IPv6 specifications say only link-local addresses are used in ICMP Redirect messages and as next hop in some routing protocols such as RIPng, so a router needs a link-local next hop for directly connected routes. Link-local addresses do not suit the BGP-4 next hop attribute rules, so a next hop sometimes has to carry both a global and a link-local address.
sections.plainLanguage: Some addresses work everywhere and some only work on your own street. Sometimes a route needs to name both kinds.

sections.title: Building the Next Hop Field
sections.content:
A BGP speaker advertises in the Network Address of Next Hop field the global IPv6 address of the next hop, potentially followed by the link-local address. The Length of Next Hop Network Address field is set to 16 when only a global address is present, or 32 when a link-local address is included too.

The link-local address is included if and only if the speaker shares a common subnet with the entity identified by the global address and with the peer the route is advertised to. Otherwise only the global address is sent, with length 16. A speaker advertising to an internal peer may therefore remove the link-local address.
sections.plainLanguage: Tell the neighbor the long-distance address. Add the local-street address only if you and the neighbor really live on the same street.

sections.title: Transport and Security
sections.content:
The TCP connections carrying BGP-4 can run over IPv4 or IPv6. BGP-4 derives implicit configuration from the address used to establish the session, so using TCP over IPv4 for IPv6 routes requires additional explicit configuration of the peer's network address. Using TCP over IPv6 also confirms IPv6 reachability between the peers.

The BGP Identifier is distinct from that. It is a 32 bit unsigned integer exchanged in the OPEN message, must be unique in the network, and should be derived from an IPv4 address. The security section says no new security issues are raised beyond those already in BGP-4.
sections.plainLanguage: The two routers can chat over the old or new kind of road, but chatting on the new road also proves the new road works.
